title: Saved by the Norton
author: Mark Bauerlein
summary: Mark Bauerlein, professor of English emeritus at Emory, recalls how declaring an English major at UCLA in 1980 meant buying the Norton Anthology of English Literature and submitting to a rigidly sequenced yearlong survey course (English 10A-10B-10C) that ran chronologically from Beowulf to Auden, graded without inflation, and organized around close textual explication. He argues the Norton served a dual function: it was the discipline's shared body of primary material ("like the Periodic Table for chemistry majors") and, just as importantly, a coherent narrative structure -- a "Grand Narrative" -- that gave the field, and by extension his own drifting nineteen-year-old life, a sense of order, dignity, and destiny he could not otherwise find. Bauerlein is candid that this was as much an existential rescue as an academic one: arriving at college nihilistic, distrustful, and unmoored, he found in the canon's chronological sweep and unquestioned authority a structure his life lacked. He contrasts this with the contemporary English major, exemplified by the University of Chicago's current "Standard Track," which requires only two of twelve courses to predate 1900 and lets students construct a personalized, non-chronological path through the discipline. His closing argument reframes the well-documented collapse of English enrollment (from one in thirteen four-year degrees in 1970 to one in sixty today) not as evidence that canon-centered instruction failed, but as evidence of an unmet "spiritual thirst" in young people for order, greatness, and charm that a curriculum without a shared canon cannot supply.
points: Bauerlein's central claim is experiential rather than pedagogical: the canon's value to him was structural and existential (a 'Grand Narrative' that ordered a chaotic life), not merely informational -- a different register of argument than typical curriculum-design defenses of the canon.

He supplies a concrete comparative data point for the canon debate: the University of Chicago's current English major requires only 2 of 12 courses to predate 1900, versus his own fully chronological, no-exceptions 10-series -- a specific before/after benchmark other classical-education writers could cite.

His reframing of the English-major enrollment collapse (1-in-13 degrees in 1970 to 1-in-60 today) as a symptom of unmet 'spiritual thirst' for order and greatness, rather than simple market forces or STEM competition, is a distinct causal claim worth flagging to readers debating the humanities' decline.

The essay models a memoir-as-argument form that pairs personal testimony (his own nihilism, his father's love of mathematical structure) with disciplinary history, giving Classical Education readers a first-person account of what canon-formation is meant to accomplish in a student's inner life, not just their transcript.
quotes: This was the dual function of the Norton. On one hand, it contained the individual objects an English major had to study. The two volumes were like the Periodic Table for chemistry majors.
There was no transcendence, no meaning in the world, nothing to live for but my meager self--and no virtue or truth that might remedy this scattered condition.
But when I opened the Norton to do homework, the world fell into place. The years had fresh meaning: 1066, 1215, 1588, 1649 and 1660, 1789, 1914.
It was a comfort to believe that a canon of great works existed and that they formed a history with direction and momentum.
Here it is, this is it, the books declared, the "ideal order." The words within had instant authority.
In 1970, English took one in thirteen of all four-year degrees in the United States. Now, it stands at one in sixty.
Teenagers in the 2020s have a spiritual thirst that is unmet by a curriculum without order and greatness and charm. A field without a bible like the Norton doesn't satisfy them.
